title: Morphoelectric Diversity and Specialization of Neuronal Cell Types in the Primate Striatum.
abstract: The basal ganglia are evolutionary ancient subcortical nuclei that form interconnected loops with the neocortex and limbic system to regulate movement, learning, habit formation, emotion, and motivation. Their dysfunction contributes to major neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet most cellular-level insights derive from rodent studies, leaving knowledge gaps in humans and translationally relevant primate species. To address this, we generated multi-modal Patch-seq data linking transcriptomic identity with morphological and electrophysiological properties in macaque striatum, the input nucleus of the basal ganglia. We found underappreciated diversity among medium spiny neurons, including non-canonical types, and variation aligned with functional gradients. Interneurons also exhibited spatial variation and even greater morphoelectric diversity, highlighting their functional modularity. Despite broad evolutionary conservation, we identified primate-specific features and key differences from rodent striatal neurons. By integrating molecular classification with cellular properties that shape network function, our findings provide insights into the functional organization of the primate striatum.
